title: Handshake slippage bench - streaming vs chunked cost/latency draft
body:
Purpose:
This is a working draft summarizing small-scale benchmarks that compare end-to-end observed latency and per-request token cost when using (a) streaming responses with an initial handshake and immediate first-chunk, versus (b) chunked-batched responses where the server waits to fill a chunk before sending. The goal: quantify the operational slippage introduced by handshake/first-byte timing under variable session sizes, and give quick knobs for console-level recommendations (SLO tiers and default route configs).

Top-level takeaways (short):
- Streaming (immediate-first-chunk) reduces median client-observed latency for short-turn interactions by ~18-32ms versus chunked-batched for small prompt+reply sizes (~32 tokens out).
- For bursty micro-interactions (90% of requests < 50 tokens), streaming yields p95 improvements of 12–28ms at modest added CPU networking overhead; cost delta per 1M requests is negligible (~$0.4–$1.2) because token billing dominates.
- For sustained long-turn sessions (>256 tokens), chunked batching recovers amortization and can cut per-token GPU cost by ~3–7% while increasing p50 latency by ~5–12ms; tradeoff depends on SLO mix.
- Handshake slippage (time between TCP/TLS handshake + initial routing and first-byte generation) is the dominant fixed overhead for very short interactions. Our app-level mitigation (lightweight handshake cache + warm-path fast-routing) reduces that overhead by ~9–12ms in our testbed.

Experiment setup (short):
- Hardware: 1x A100-80GB host (dedicated test rig), driver stack matching prod 2029-06 release.
- Runtime: Redwood runtime branch bench/handshake-2029 (PR 478), with two server configs: streaming=true (immediate first chunk size=32 tokens) and streaming=false (chunk-size=64, server waits to fill or 5ms timeout).
- Models: open-llama-70B-8bit, rw-13B-fp16 (representative heavy and mid models).
- Client mix: synthetic trace generator mimicking conversational microprofile: {70% requests 8–40 tokens response, 25% requests 40–200t, 5% >200t}.
- Metrics collected: client-observed latency (p50,p90,p95,p99), server CPU/network overhead, GPU utilization, token throughput, cost estimate (GPU-time mapped to $/token using reserved capacity rate table).
- Runs: 6x 10-minute windows for each config/model combination, warmed up for 3 minutes.

Raw-ish results (representative aggregated numbers):
- Model: rw-13B-fp16, client mix above
  - streaming=true: p50=38ms, p90=92ms, p95=132ms, p99=312ms, avg tokens/req=36, GPU-util=62%
  - streaming=false: p50=52ms, p90=104ms, p95=148ms, p99=350ms, avg tokens/req=36, GPU-util=66%
  - delta streaming v chunked: p50 -14ms (-27%), p95 -16ms (-10.8%), p99 -38ms (-10.8%)

- Model: open-llama-70B-8bit
  - streaming=true: p50=58ms, p90=126ms, p95=186ms, p99=422ms, avg tokens/req=36, GPU-util=74%
  - streaming=false: p50=74ms, p90=142ms, p95=200ms, p99=470ms, avg tokens/req=36, GPU-util=78%
  - delta: p50 -16ms (-21.6%), p95 -14ms (-7%)

ASCII microcharts (p50/p95 trend across chunk-timeouts):
  chunk-timeout-ms  | p50 (ms) streaming=false | p95 (ms) streaming=false
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  1                  | 49                      | 135
  5                  | 52                      | 148   <-- default used in main chunked run
  10                 | 58                      | 162
  20                 | 68                      | 186

Network/CPU overhead notes (short):
- Streaming mode increases server-side net-packets-per-request by ~12% (more frequent small writes), CPU sys-time up by ~4–6% at moderate QPS. For most routes this is acceptable; for extreme multi-tenant edge nodes the increased syscall rate can slightly reduce top throughput.
- Chunked mode gives slightly better packing efficiency: lower NIC interrupts and better TCP coalescing, reducing CPU sys-time but increasing TTFB (time to first byte).

Cost mapping (back-of-envelope, per 1M requests with our reserved capacity rate table):
- rw-13B-fp16:
  - streaming: estimated infra cost = $1,840 per 1M requests (dominant: GPU-time tokens).
  - chunked: estimated infra cost = $1,822 per 1M requests (savings mainly from slightly higher GPU throughput efficiency).
  - delta: chunked saves ~$18 per 1M requests (~1%).
- open-llama-70B-8bit:
  - streaming: $3,920 per 1M requests
  - chunked: $3,879 per 1M requests
  - delta: ~$41 per 1M requests (~1%)
Notes: the delta grows smaller when real KV-cache hitrates increase (prefix reuse) because per-token generation dominates.

Percentile breakdown (example table style, text):
- rw-13B-fp16 (streaming=true): p10=22ms, p25=28ms, p50=38ms, p75=61ms, p90=92ms, p95=132ms, p99=312ms
- rw-13B-fp16 (streaming=false): p10=26ms, p25=33ms, p50=52ms, p75=71ms, p90=104ms, p95=148ms, p99=350ms

Interpretation / candidate console defaults:
1) Default route (free-tier / interactive defaults): streaming=true, first-chunk-size=32, handshake-cache=enabled. Rationale: most user-facing micro-interactions are short; better p50/p95 improves perceived responsiveness.
2) Bulk / high-throughput routes (embedding, async batch): streaming=false, chunk-size=128 or 256, chunk-timeout 10–20ms to favor batching. Rationale: maximize packing and reduce per-token $ for heavy workloads.
3) Enterprise SLO tier: expose a toggle: prefer-lower-latency (streaming) vs prefer-lower-cost (chunked) with advisory cost delta estimates.

Operational knobs we tried and their impact (notes):
- Handshake-cache (per-client TLS session resumption + routing cache): reduces fixed 1st-byte overhead by ~9–12ms on average. Low-risk to enable in console.
- Adaptive chunking (start streaming if request-length < 64 tokens else chunk): reduces both p50 and keeps packing for long sessions; complexity: needs fast length-estimation from client.
- Server-side coalescer (aggregate small writes into single syscall every 1ms): recovers ~6–8ms of CPU overhead when streaming under load; minor code uplift.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Need production-scale validate across multi-node, multi-tenant edges: does streaming amplify slot fragmentation for small tenants? (JIRA-1024 covers a follow-up test).
- Measure real-world client-side UX: run A/B in canary for chat prompt templates where users send many short messages (customer cohort sample).
- Add variants including HTTP/3 QUIC runs (we only tested HTTP/2 and direct TCP). Early Q3 tests planned.

Appendix: quick-run recipe for replicating locally:
1) Checkout runtime branch bench/handshake-2029; run docker-compose bench-rw13 with env RUN_MODE=streaming or RUN_MODE=chunked.
2) Start trace generator: python3 loadgen.py --mix micro --qps 350 --duration 600 --firstchunk 32 (script in repo /bench/loadgen).
3) Collect results: ./tools/collect-latency.sh > out.json; use analyze_latency.ipynb to generate percentile tables.

Contact: Maya Chen (mchen@redwood.ai) — ping channel #bench-handshake for quick sync.

Quick status notes: draft, needs platform team sign-off on network/cpu overhead impact before recommending as default for edge-hosted routes.

----
Notes-to-self (raw):
- observed that open-llama p99 tail more sensitive to NIC bursts; experiment with larger socket buffers.
- consider client-side first-chunk hint (client advertises expected response size) to enable adaptive chunking without extra RTT.
